# Squeeze Harder, Say "Same": Physical Effort Lowers Older Adults' Reports of Perceptual Differences {#sec-ch3}

```{r ch3-setup}
#| include: false
source(file.path("chapter3", "setup.R"), local = knitr::knit_global())
```

## Abstract {.unnumbered}

Everyday perception often happens while the body is working, and combining demands is more costly with age. Whether physical effort changes what older adults perceive or only how readily they report a change, and whether pupil size tracks that effect, is unknown. Sixty-eight older adults judged whether two tones or two visual gratings were the same or different while squeezing a handgrip at 5% or 40% of maximum strength. Mixed-effects models of the psychometric function, the probability of reporting "different" across stimulus differences and when the stimuli were identical, tested whether high physical effort shifted the criterion for reporting a difference, reduced sensitivity, or imposed a cost that grew with task difficulty, and related pupil size before and after the second stimulus (the probe) to the judgment. Under high physical effort, participants reported a difference less often. The reduction was about as large when the stimuli were identical as when they differed, although not reliable on identical trials alone, consistent with a more conservative criterion. It was slightly larger for the smallest differences, but sensitivity did not decline overall. Pupil size during the grip did not differ reliably between physical effort levels, and the smaller pupil response to the probe under high physical effort coincided with grip release. A larger pupil before the probe was weakly associated with lower sensitivity, and no pupil measure tracked the criterion. In older adults, high physical effort appears to change mainly how readily a difference is reported rather than how well it is perceived.

## Introduction

Everyday perception often takes place while the body is working, which combines two demands: the physical effort of a motor task and the task difficulty of a perceptual judgment. Older adults show larger dual-task costs than younger adults [@verhaeghen2003], and holding an effortful isometric grip lowered older adults' visual working-memory accuracy when distractors were present [@Azer2023-ft]. What physical effort does to a perceptual judgment, and whether its effect depends on task difficulty, is less clear.

A psychometric function relates the size of the difference between two stimuli, here called the offset, to the probability of reporting "different." Its slope indexes sensitivity, how sharply that probability rises with the offset, and catch trials, on which the two stimuli are identical, show how often a difference is reported when there is none. Two accounts describe how physical effort could change the function [@macmillan2005detection; @prins2016psychophysics]. In the first, holding a demanding grip draws attention away from the stimuli. Attention enhances the representation of attended stimuli and increases perceptual sensitivity [@Carrasco2011-wc], so less of it would make the sensory evidence noisier, lower sensitivity, and flatten the function; physical effort would then degrade what older adults perceive. In the second, physical effort changes the decision rather than the evidence. Motor costs can bias perceptual decisions: observers chose a response less often when making it required more effort, without any change in sensitivity [@hagura2017], and changed their minds less often when changing a decision required a larger movement [@burk2014]. If a concurrent physical demand similarly raises the evidence observers require before reporting a change, the criterion shifts: the function moves toward larger offsets without becoming shallower, and "different" responses also become rarer on catch trials (@fig-ch3-predictions, panels A and B). Physical effort would then change how readily older adults report a difference, not what they perceive.

A third, the capacity account, holds that concurrent demands compete for limited processing resources [@Kahneman1973-jw; @Wickens2008-pj]. If a difficult judgment and high physical effort draw on the same resources, the cost of physical effort should be largest when the judgment is hardest, here at the smallest offsets, and absent on catch trials, where there is no difference to miss (@fig-ch3-predictions, panel C). This differs from the sensitivity account: noisier evidence flattens the whole function, so its cost grows as the offset grows, whereas a limit on shared resources concentrates the cost where the judgment is hardest. Chapter 2 [@Dastgheib2026-crpi] tested this account in younger adults performing a working-memory task and two discrimination tasks, one auditory and one visual. Harder trials were less accurate in every task and slower in both discrimination tasks, high physical effort slowed responses only in the visual discrimination task, and task difficulty and physical effort did not interact on any measure. High physical effort also enlarged the pupil response in all three tasks, whereas task difficulty did not change it, and the two again did not interact. Whether the same holds in older adults has not been tested.

(A) Criterion account: fewer \"different\" responses by the same amount on the probit scale at every offset and on catch trials, with the shape of the function unchanged. (B) Sensitivity account: a shallower function, with no fewer \"different\" responses on catch trials. (C) Capacity account: a reduction concentrated at the smallest offsets and absent at the largest offset and on catch trials. The same predictions are shown as effects on the model's scale in @fig-ch3-effort-by-offset, panel A."

In the older adults studied here, @sun2026handgrip fitted a psychometric function to each participant's responses in each task and physical effort condition and compared thresholds, the offset needed to report "different" on a set proportion of trials, and slopes between physical effort levels. High physical effort raised thresholds, reliably in the auditory task and less robustly in the visual task, without changing slopes or response times. Sun et al. read this as a more conservative criterion for "different," the pattern of the criterion account, and noted that it did not match the dual-task cost that an effortful grip imposes on older adults' working memory [@Azer2023-ft], the kind of cost the capacity account predicts. Two questions remained open. With 75 trials per physical effort level, a single participant's slope is uncertain, so per-participant fits cannot show whether the cost of physical effort concentrates on the smallest offsets. And that analysis did not relate the effect of physical effort to the pupil, which Sun et al. identified as the next step. A model of all trials, with participants as random effects, estimates directly how the effect of physical effort changes across offsets and on catch trials, and it can relate pupil size on each trial to the judgment on that trial.

Pupil size offers a test of these accounts beyond choices. It increases with task difficulty [@Beatty1982-wg; @Van_der_Wel2018-ko] and with physical effort [@Zenon2014-ze], and the two demands can be separated here because they were manipulated independently and occur at different times: the grip begins several seconds before the stimuli to be judged. Each account makes its own pupil prediction. If physical effort and the judgment compete for limited resources, as the capacity account holds, pupil size during the grip should be larger under high physical effort, and the task-evoked pupil response (TEPR) that follows the probe should grow as the offset shrinks. If sensitivity varies with the state in which an observer meets the stimulus, as the sensitivity account implies, trials with a larger pupil just before the probe should show a shallower function, because larger pupil size has been linked to more variable evidence accumulation from trial to trial [@murphy2014pupil]. If physical effort shifts the criterion, pupil size should track the rate of "different" responses: decision-related dilation varies with the upcoming choice and with an observer's bias [@degee2014], and larger phasic responses have been associated with smaller choice biases [@deGee2020pupil]. The TEPR is therefore informative about the criterion, although it partly reflects the response and the grip release as well as the decision. In older adults the pupil is smaller and its range of dilation narrower [@winn1994; @piquado2010], so these effects may be harder to detect.

This chapter asks two questions. The first is how high physical effort changes the judgment. The criterion account predicts fewer "different" responses by a similar amount at every offset and on catch trials, the sensitivity account predicts a shallower function, and the capacity account predicts a reduction that is largest at the smallest offsets and absent on catch trials. In a probit model of all trials, these predictions correspond to a physical effort effect that is the same across offsets and on catch trials, a negative offset × physical effort interaction, and a positive offset × physical effort interaction together with a positive catch × physical effort interaction that cancels the reduction on catch trials (@fig-ch3-effort-by-offset, panel A). The accounts are not mutually exclusive, and because the model estimates each term, it can show whether the data combine them. The second question is whether pupil size shows the pattern each account predicts: for the capacity account, a larger pupil during the grip under high physical effort and a larger TEPR at smaller offsets; for the sensitivity account, a shallower function on trials with a larger pupil just before the probe; and for the criterion account, an association between pupil size before or after the probe and the rate of "different" responses.

## Methods

### Participants and trials {#sec-ch3-participants}

Recruitment, exclusions, and demographics are those of @sun2026handgrip. Participants gave written informed consent and were paid, and procedures were approved by the University of California, Riverside Institutional Review Board. The behavioral analysis uses the cleaned trial file of that study: `r v_int("m1_nobs")` trials from `r v_int("m1_n_participants")` participants (`r v_int("m1_n_adt")` auditory, `r v_int("m1_n_vdt")` visual), of whom `r v_words("n_one_task")` completed only one task (@tbl-ch3-demographics). In that file, trials were excluded when grip force was not maintained within the target range (1–15% of MVC for low physical effort, 30–55% for high physical effort) for at least two-thirds of the 2- to 3-s period after trial onset, or when the response was missing, faster than 200 ms after the response prompt, or part of a run with more than 90% identical responses; about 90% of trials remained [@sun2026handgrip].

The pupil analyses use a subset of these trials: those with a recording that passed the checks described under Pupillometry (@sec-ch3-pupillometry). The task-evoked models (M3 and M4) use `r v_int("m3_nobs")` trials from `r v_int("m3_n_participants")` participants (`r v_int("m3_n_adt")` auditory, `r v_int("m3_n_vdt")` visual), and the grip-period model (M2) uses `r v_int("m2_nobs")` trials from `r v_int("m2_n_participants")` participants. Of the `r v_int("m1_n_participants")` participants, `r v_int("n_no_tepr")` contributed no trials to the task-evoked models because no recording existed or fewer than 20 trials passed the checks (@tbl-ch3-pupil-flow).

### Task, stimuli, and apparatus {#sec-ch3-task-paradigm}

Participants completed an auditory and a visual same–different task in the scanner, one task per session, in counterbalanced order. The tasks were adapted from the auditory and visual discrimination tasks of Chapter 2, with different offsets and timing. On each trial they held a left-hand grip at 5% (low physical effort) or 40% (high physical effort) of their maximum voluntary contraction (MVC), heard or saw a standard and then a comparison stimulus, the probe (the target in Chapter 2), judged whether the two were the same or different, and rated their confidence (@fig-ch3-paradigm). The inter-trial interval was 1.5–4.5 s. From squeeze onset, the standard began at 3.75 s and the probe at 4.35 s, each lasting 0.1 s. At probe offset (4.45 s), a change in border color cued participants to release the grip. The same–different response window ran from 4.70 to 7.70 s, and the confidence window followed. Each task had five blocks of 30 trials, in which the five probe levels and the two physical effort levels were crossed, three trials per combination, in pseudorandom order.

stopifnot(file.exists(paradigm_path))

The auditory standard was a 1,000-Hz tone, and the probe was identical or 8, 16, 32, or 64 Hz higher. The visual standard was a Gabor patch (1.5 cycles/degree, Michelson contrast 0.20, 4°), and the probe was identical or had a contrast 0.06, 0.12, 0.24, or 0.48 higher. Trials with an identical probe are catch trials.

Stimuli were presented with Psychtoolbox 3.0.18 [@Brainard1997-fk] in MATLAB R2022b on a PROPixx projector (VPixx Technologies; 480 Hz, 1920 × 1080) viewed through a head-coil mirror (effective viewing distance 12 cm), and sounds were delivered through MRI-compatible earbuds. Grip force was recorded with an MRI-compatible dynamometer (Current Designs; 100 Hz) and pupil diameter with a TRACKPixx binocular eye tracker (VPixx Technologies; 2,000 Hz). MVC was the mean of three maximal squeezes, measured in an initial session outside the scanner and again in the scanner, and the value measured in the scanner set the 5% and 40% targets.

### Pupillometry {#sec-ch3-pupillometry}

Blinks and other artifacts were removed with ET-Remove-Artifacts [@mather2020isometric]. Pupil diameter, in arbitrary units, was analyzed at 250 Hz on a time axis that starts 3 s before squeeze onset; trials whose recording did not match that axis were excluded (@sec-ch3-supp-pupil). Four measures were taken from each trial. The pre-squeeze baseline is the mean over the 0.5 s before squeeze onset. The grip-period mean is the mean over 1.0–4.35 s after squeeze onset, minus the pre-squeeze baseline. Pre-probe pupil is the mean over the 0.5 s before probe onset (3.85–4.35 s); because this window follows the standard (3.75–3.85 s), it contains the early response to the standard. The TEPR is the mean over 4.65–7.65 s minus pre-probe pupil. Each measure required at least half of its samples to be valid, and a participant entered a pupil model only with at least 20 such trials in that task.

The TEPR window begins after probe offset, so grip release, the release cue, the response screen, and the button press all fall inside it. Of the four measures, only pre-probe pupil precedes the probe.

In the models that relate pupil size to the judgment, each pupil measure was split into a state and a trait component within that model's sample, the standard way to separate within-person from between-person effects in multilevel models [@curran2011; @enders2007]. State is the trial value minus the participant's mean for that task, divided by the standard deviation pooled across participant × task cells, so its coefficient reflects trial-to-trial fluctuation within a participant. Trait is the participant's mean for that task on the same scale, so its coefficient reflects stable differences between participants. Relations between pupil size and perceptual decisions have been reported at both levels [@murphy2014pupil].

### Models {#sec-ch3-models}

The behavioral outcome was a "different" response. Catch was coded 1 on catch trials and 0 otherwise, and the centered offset was −1.5, −0.5, 0.5, and 1.5 on the four nonzero offsets and 0 on catch trials. Physical effort (low = −0.5, high = +0.5) and task (auditory = −0.5, visual = +0.5) were sum-coded, so each coefficient is the high-minus-low or visual-minus-auditory difference on the model's link scale.

Models were fit in R [@R] with lme4 `r v("lme4_version")` and lmerTest `r v("lmerTest_version")` [@bates2015fitting; @kuznetsova2017lmerTest]. Each started from the maximal random-effects structure [@Barr2013-maximal] and was simplified in fixed steps until the fit was neither singular nor flagged by the optimizer [@bates2015fitting]; the steps are listed in @sec-ch3-supp-models. The models were specified before they were fit; the study was not pre-registered, and the reading of the sign of the offset × physical effort interaction as a test of the capacity account was added after the results were known (@sec-ch3-disc-criterion).

**Behavior (M1).** All `r v_int("m1_nobs")` trials were analyzed with a probit regression of "different" responses on catch, centered offset, physical effort, and task, with all estimable interactions among them; catch × offset terms are not estimable because the centered offset is 0 on catch trials. Each participant had a random slope for catch, centered offset, physical effort, and task. Because the centered offset is 0 both on catch trials and at the average nonzero offset, the physical effort coefficient is the effect of physical effort at the average offset, and the catch × physical effort interaction is how much the effect on catch trials differs from it. The criterion account predicts a negative physical effort coefficient and neither a catch × physical effort nor an offset × physical effort interaction. The sensitivity account predicts a negative offset × physical effort interaction. The capacity account predicts a positive offset × physical effort interaction and a positive catch × physical effort interaction that cancels the physical effort coefficient on catch trials.

**Grip-period pupil (M2).** Linear model of the grip-period mean on physical effort, task, and a physical effort × task interaction, with a by-participant random slope for physical effort. It tests whether high physical effort enlarged the pupil during the grip. The reported manipulation check is grip force, not pupil [@sun2026handgrip].

**Task-evoked pupil (M3).** Linear model of the TEPR mean on physical effort, task, and a physical effort × task interaction, and on catch and centered offset, with by-participant random slopes for physical effort and offset. It tests whether the TEPR differed with physical effort and with offset.

**Pupil and sensitivity (M4).** Probit models on the same `r v_int("m4a_nobs")` trials as M3. The primary predictor is pre-probe pupil (M4a). The secondary predictor is the TEPR mean (M4b). Both include state and trait, and both keep physical effort and task so the pupil coefficients are estimated within levels of physical effort and task. The state interactions are offset × state (the slope term) and catch × state. A negative slope term means a shallower function.

**Missing pupil data (M5).** A control model tested whether pupil data were more often usable at one physical effort level (@sec-ch3-supp-pupil).

### Statistical inference {#sec-ch3-inference}

Effects are reported with Wald 95% confidence intervals and two-sided *p* values; for the linear models, degrees of freedom are Satterthwaite approximations. No correction was applied across models, because each model tests a different question. No equivalence bound was set, so a nonsignificant effect is reported as its estimate and interval, not as evidence that there was no effect.

## Results

### Physical effort and "different" responses {#sec-ch3-behavior}

Under high physical effort, the mean proportion of "different" responses was lower at every offset in both tasks except the 0.24 contrast offset in the visual task (@fig-ch3-p-diff). On catch trials, the proportion of "different" responses was `r v("catch_adt_p")` in the auditory task and `r v("catch_vdt_p")` in the visual task. Responding was near ceiling at the largest offset (auditory, `r v("top_adt_p")`; visual, `r v("top_vdt_p")`), where the high-minus-low difference in proportion was `r v("level4_adt_diff_prop")` in the auditory task and `r v("level4_vdt_diff_prop")` in the visual task.

### Pupil and sensitivity {#sec-ch3-coupling}

## Discussion

We asked whether high physical effort changes older adults' perceptual judgments by lowering sensitivity or by shifting the criterion for reporting a difference, and whether pupil size tracks either effect. Under high physical effort, older adults reported a difference less often in both tasks, by a similar amount on catch trials as at the average offset, although the catch-trial estimate was uncertain on its own, and the psychometric function did not become shallower. The reduction was slightly larger at the smallest offsets. Pupil size during the grip differed little between physical effort levels, the TEPR was smaller under high physical effort, and only pupil size before the probe was associated, weakly, with sensitivity.

### Mainly a criterion shift, not a loss of sensitivity {#sec-ch3-disc-criterion}

The Introduction set out three accounts of how physical effort could change a perceptual judgment, and the data rule out the first of them, a loss of sensitivity. The psychometric function did not become shallower under high physical effort, and the interval of the offset × physical effort interaction excluded the negative values the sensitivity account predicts. Whatever attention the grip drew away from the stimuli did not measurably degrade the precision of the evidence. That contrasts with the working-memory cost of an effortful grip in older adults [@Azer2023-ft], perhaps because holding items in memory against distractors depends more on attentional control than a comparison of two brief stimuli does. The reduction on catch trials was similar in size to the reduction at the average offset, the pattern the criterion account predicts [@macmillan2005detection], and it agrees with the higher thresholds and unchanged slopes that @sun2026handgrip found with per-participant fits in the same cohort. The catch trials, however, do not separate the criterion account from the capacity account. Taken alone, the reduction on catch trials had an interval that included zero (@fig-ch3-effort-by-offset, panel B), and the interval of the catch × physical effort interaction also includes the value the capacity account predicts, no reduction on catch trials. The criterion reading therefore rests on the direction and size of the catch-trial estimate together with the converging per-participant result.

The effect of physical effort was largest at the smallest offsets and close to zero at the largest, a positive offset × physical effort interaction (@fig-ch3-effort-by-offset, panel B). That is the direction the capacity account predicts [@Kahneman1973-jw; @Wickens2008-pj], but the cost was small and its interval nearly reached zero. Because a pure criterion shift predicts no such interaction, the criterion account alone does not describe the data either; the pattern is closer to a criterion shift with a small cost concentrated on the hardest judgments. Three cautions apply. The analysis plan specified this term as a test of a shallower function, and reading a positive term as support for the capacity account was added after the results were known. Responding was near ceiling at the largest offset, where a probit model without a lapse rate can express a shrinking difference as a steeper slope. And the gradient was steeper in the visual task than in the auditory task, although the offset × physical effort × task interaction was not significant. That difference echoes Chapter 2, in which high physical effort slowed responses only in the visual discrimination task [@Dastgheib2026-crpi], while the threshold increase reported by @sun2026handgrip was more robust in the auditory task, so whether physical effort affects the two modalities through different routes remains open. Chapter 2 found no interaction between task difficulty and physical effort in younger adults; whether the small cost seen here reflects age cannot be decided without a younger group measured in the same way.

### Why the criterion might shift {#sec-ch3-disc-why}

If the criterion did shift, three mechanisms could produce it. The first places the shift in the decision. Motor costs can shift perceptual decisions: a costlier response is chosen less often without any change in sensitivity [@hagura2017], and a decision is revised less often when revising it requires a larger movement [@burk2014]. A concurrent physical demand may similarly raise the evidence observers require before reporting a change. In the same cohort, high physical effort also improved metacognitive efficiency, an effect that appeared to be driven by lower confidence on errors at the easiest auditory offset [@sun2026handgrip]. A decision state that is both more conservative and better at registering its own errors fits a criterion shift better than degraded input, although the two physical effort effects did not covary across participants [@sun2026handgrip], so they may not share one mechanism. The second mechanism is that physical effort acts on the decision through processes indexed by the pupil. Decision-related pupil dilation varies with the upcoming choice and with an observer's bias [@degee2014], and larger phasic responses have been associated with smaller choice biases [@deGee2020pupil], which is why the Introduction predicted that pupil size would track the rate of "different" responses under the criterion account. Here neither pre-probe pupil nor the TEPR predicted that rate, so trial-to-trial changes in pupil size gave no sign of carrying the physical effort effect. The third mechanism places the shift at the response. In @hagura2017, the bias followed the cost attached to a particular response; here "different" was always reported with the right index finger and "same" with the right middle finger, and a left-hand grip could bias right-hand responding toward one finger. Choices alone cannot separate these mechanisms. Chapter 4 uses response times to test whether the shift lies in how the evidence is evaluated, in how much evidence is required, or in a bias set before the stimulus.

### Physical effort and pupil size {#sec-ch3-disc-pupil}

The capacity account predicted a larger pupil during the grip under high physical effort and a larger TEPR at smaller offsets. Neither appeared. Pupil size during the grip did not differ significantly between physical effort levels. In younger adults, by contrast, high physical effort enlarged the pupil response in every task (Chapter 2), although the measures are not directly comparable: Chapter 2 summarized the pupil from trial onset to the response window, including the response to the probe, and recorded it in a quiet, dimly lit laboratory rather than a scanner. Several features of this sample could weaken the effect. Older adults have smaller pupils and a narrower range of dilation [@winn1994; @piquado2010]. In the difference waveform, the two physical effort levels were separated only intermittently during the grip and most consistently in the last second before the probe, including the pre-probe window (@fig-ch3-pupil-timecourse, panel B), so a window that averages over the whole grip period also averages over periods in which they did not differ. The effect of physical effort also varied considerably across participants, and only `r v_int("m2_n_participants")` of the `r v_int("m1_n_participants")` participants contributed to that model.

The TEPR was smaller under high physical effort, but this difference cannot be attributed to processing of the probe. Grip release, its cue, and the button press fall inside the TEPR window, and releasing a grip held at high physical effort differs from releasing one held at low physical effort. The TEPR is also measured from pre-probe pupil, which the difference waveform shows was larger under high physical effort (@fig-ch3-pupil-timecourse, panel B), and evoked responses tend to be smaller when baseline pupil size is larger [@Gilzenrat2010-ye]; after the probe, the difference between physical effort levels shrank, to near zero in the auditory task and to a few brief intervals in the visual task (@fig-ch3-pupil-timecourse, panel B). The TEPR did not differ with offset or on catch trials (@fig-ch3-pupil-timecourse, panel C), just as task difficulty did not change the whole-trial pupil response in Chapter 2. Taken with the small behavioral cost at the smallest offsets, the pupil data give the capacity account little support: if physical effort and the judgment had competed for the resources the pupil indexes [@Kahneman1973-jw; @Beatty1982-wg], the pupil should have registered both demands, although the reduced dilation range of older adults limits how strongly this null can be read.

### Pre-probe pupil and sensitivity {#sec-ch3-disc-preprobe}

The sensitivity account predicted that a larger pupil just before the probe would accompany a shallower function, and that was the one pupil association observed: on trials on which pupil size before the probe was larger than the participant's mean, the psychometric function was shallower (@fig-ch3-pupil-coupling). The direction matches the link between larger pupil size and more variable evidence accumulation [@murphy2014pupil]. Because physical effort itself did not lower sensitivity, however, this association does not explain the effect of physical effort; it shows that sensitivity varied with the state in which observers met the probe. The evidence is also weak: the interval reaches zero, and the pre-probe window contains the early response to the standard. One interpretation comes from adaptive gain theory, which links pupil size to the activity of the locus coeruleus–noradrenergic (LC–NE) system [@Aston-Jones2005-dg; @joshi2016]. In that theory, a larger baseline pupil accompanies a less task-focused state [@Gilzenrat2010-ye], and performance is best at intermediate baseline pupil sizes [@Murphy2011-nr]. Isometric handgrip engages the noradrenergic system [@mather2020isometric], and the locus coeruleus is among the brain structures most vulnerable to aging [@mather2016], so a route from physical effort to perception through the LC–NE system is plausible in older adults. This study, however, neither manipulated nor analyzed locus coeruleus activity during the task, and pupil size also covaries with activity outside the locus coeruleus [@joshi2016]. The association is therefore a hypothesis for a study with a pre-stimulus baseline free of other stimuli, not a finding this chapter rests on. The TEPR, summarized as a mean or as an area (@sec-ch3-supp-robust), was associated with neither the slope nor the rate of "different" responses.

### Limitations {#sec-ch3-disc-limits}

Several limitations qualify these conclusions. The pupil windows were constrained by the trial sequence: grip release, its cue, and the button press fall inside the task-evoked window, and the pre-probe window contains the early response to the standard. The response mapping was not counterbalanced, so a bias tied to one finger cannot be ruled out. With two physical effort levels, the data cannot describe a dose–response relation or test an inverted-U relation between physical effort and performance. The chapter has no younger group, so no effect can be attributed to age. Locus coeruleus activity was imaged but is not analyzed here. Data were collected in an MRI scanner, which constrains luminance, posture, and noise, and pupil size was recorded in arbitrary units. Pupil data were missing or unusable for `r v_int("n_no_tepr")` of the `r v_int("m1_n_participants")` participants, and trials at high physical effort were slightly more likely to be usable (@sec-ch3-supp-pupil), although every pupil model included physical effort. In the models that related pupil size to the judgment (M4a and M4b), the physical effort terms had the same sign as in M1, but their intervals included zero (@sec-ch3-supp-models). The behavioral model had no lapse rate, so the positive offset × physical effort interaction cannot be separated from a ceiling effect.

### Conclusion {#sec-ch3-disc-conclusion}

The Introduction set out three accounts of how physical effort could change older adults' perceptual judgments. The data rule out a general loss of sensitivity, favor a criterion shift, and leave room for a small capacity-like cost on the hardest judgments, an ambiguity that a model with a lapse rate or a design with more trials near threshold could resolve. The pupil predictions fared similarly: pupil size during the grip and after the probe did not show the pattern the capacity account predicts, pupil size before the probe tracked sensitivity only weakly, and no pupil measure tracked the criterion. For older adults, then, high physical effort appears to change mainly how readily a difference is reported rather than how well it is perceived. That distinction matters wherever older adults must notice a change while exerting themselves: a more conservative criterion predicts more missed changes when the evidence is weak, without implying that perception itself is impaired. A study that counterbalances the response mapping, uses more than two physical effort levels, measures a pre-stimulus baseline free of other stimuli, and models confidence alongside choice could separate the decision and response mechanisms and test whether pupil size before a stimulus predicts discrimination. In this chapter, high physical effort made older adults less likely to report a difference, in a pattern that favors a criterion shift toward "same," and pupil size did not account for that change.
